2-5.title: Right and Wrong!
2-5.description: Learning to be kind, fair, and tell the truth!

en.title: Right and Wrong!
en.welcome: Hi thinker! Do you have a brain? Yes! We use our brains to think about BIG questions. Like... what is 'Good'?
en.mainContent:
**Fairness:** Imagine you have a cookie. Your friend has no cookie. Is that fair? Sharing makes it fair! Fairness means everyone gets a turn.

**Kindness:** If your friend falls down, do you laugh? No! That is mean. You help them up. That is **Kind**. Being kind makes hearts happy.

**Truth:** Did you eat the cookie? If you say 'No' but you have crumbs on your face... that is a lie! Telling the **Truth** means saying what really happened. It makes people trust you.

**Why?** Philosophers are people who ask 'Why?' 
*   Why is the sky blue?
*   Why do we have to sleep?
*   Why should I be nice?
Asking 'Why' helps us learn!

**The Golden Rule:** Treat others how YOU want to be treated. 
*   Do you like to be hit? No. So don't hit.
*   Do you like hugs? Yes. So give hugs!
It's a magic rule for being a good person.
keyPoints: Fairness means sharing and taking turns
Kindness means helping, not hurting
Truth means saying what really happened
Philosophers ask 'Why?' to learn
The Golden Rule: Treat others how you want to be treated
interactionPrompts: If you find a toy that isn't yours, what should you do?
Show me a 'Kind' face. Now show me a 'Thinking' face.
Why is it good to share?
en.wisdomMoment: When you are kind, you are a superhero. Your superpower is Love.
en.core_metaphor: The Golden Rule is a mirror
en.cta: Do one kind thing today (share a toy, give a hug). How did it feel?
en.summary: You learned about Fairness, Kindness, Truth, Asking Why, and the Golden Rule!

6-12.title: Philosophy 101: How to Think
6-12.description: Logic, fallacies, and the difference between facts and opinions

en.title: Philosophy 101: How to Think
en.welcome: Philosophy means 'Love of Wisdom.' It's not about knowing the answers; it's about asking the right questions. Let's exercise our brains.
en.mainContent:
**Fact vs. Opinion:**
*   **Fact:** Something that is true for everyone. 'The sun is hot.' '2+2=4.'
*   **Opinion:** How you feel about something. 'Broccoli is yucky.' 'Blue is the best color.'
You can't argue with facts, but you can disagree on opinions!

**Logic:** Thinking clearly. 
*   *Syllogism:* 
    1. All humans are mortal (will die).
    2. Socrates is a human.
    3. Therefore, Socrates is mortal.
This is logical! If 1 and 2 are true, 3 MUST be true.

**Logical Fallacies (Bad Thinking):**
*   **Ad Hominem:** Attacking the person, not the idea. 'You're wrong because you're ugly!' (Bad logic!)
*   **Bandwagon:** 'Everyone is doing it, so it must be right.' (Nope! Everyone could be wrong).

**Ethics (Right vs. Wrong):**
*   **The Trolley Problem:** A trolley is coming. It will hit 5 people. You can pull a lever to switch tracks, but it will hit 1 person. What do you do? Save 5 or save 1? There is no easy answer!

**Socrates:** A famous philosopher who said, 'The only true wisdom is in knowing you know nothing.' He asked questions until people realized they didn't know the answers. Be like Socrates: Ask questions!
keyPoints: Philosophy is the 'Love of Wisdom'
Facts are true for everyone; Opinions are personal feelings
Logic helps us think clearly (Syllogisms)
Fallacies are mistakes in thinking (Ad Hominem, Bandwagon)
Ethics explores difficult choices (Trolley Problem)
interactionPrompts: Is 'Chocolate is the best' a Fact or Opinion?
What would you do in the Trolley Problem? Why?
Why is it important to admit when you don't know something?
en.wisdomMoment: An unexamined life is not worth living. (Socrates). Think about why you do what you do.
en.core_metaphor: Logic is a tool kit for the mind
en.cta: Catch yourself having an opinion today. Ask: 'Is this a fact or just what I think?'
en.summary: You've learned about Fact vs. Opinion, Logic, Fallacies, Ethics (Trolley Problem), and Socrates.

13-17.title: Stoicism & Existentialism: Finding Meaning
13-17.description: Ancient and modern philosophies for navigating life's challenges

en.title: Stoicism & Existentialism: Finding Meaning
en.welcome: Life is hard. You will face pain, loss, and confusion. Philosophy is the armor you wear to survive it. Let's look at two powerful schools of thought.
en.mainContent:
**Stoicism (The Ancient Greeks/Romans):** Focus on what you can control.
*   **Dichotomy of Control:** You control your thoughts and actions. You DO NOT control other people, the weather, or the past. Stop worrying about what you can't control.
*   **Marcus Aurelius:** A Roman Emperor who wrote to himself: 'You have power over your mind - not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.'
*   **Amor Fati:** Love your fate. Don't just bear it; embrace it. If it rains, love the rain.

**Existentialism (The Moderns):** You are free to create your own meaning.
*   **Existence precedes Essence:** You are born first (Existence), and then you define who you are (Essence). There is no pre-written script.
*   **The Absurd:** Life has no inherent meaning. This sounds scary, but it's liberating! It means YOU get to decide what matters. You are the artist of your life.
*   **Jean-Paul Sartre:** 'Man is condemned to be free.' You are responsible for your choices. No excuses.

**Nihilism vs. Existentialism:**
*   **Nihilism:** Life has no meaning, so nothing matters. (Depressing).
*   **Existentialism:** Life has no meaning, so I can create my own! (Empowering).

**Virtue Ethics (Aristotle):** Happiness comes from being a good person (Virtuous). Courage, Temperance, Wisdom, Justice. Practice these like muscles.
keyPoints: Stoicism: Focus only on what you can control (thoughts/actions)
Existentialism: You are free to create your own meaning
Amor Fati: Love your fate, whatever it is
Nihilism (nothing matters) vs Existentialism (I decide what matters)
Virtue Ethics: Happiness comes from character
interactionPrompts: What is something you are worrying about that you can't control?
If life has no pre-written meaning, what meaning will you give yours?
Which virtue do you want to strengthen (Courage, Wisdom, etc.)?
en.wisdomMoment: He who has a 'why' to live can bear almost any 'how'. (Nietzsche). Find your Why.
en.core_metaphor: Philosophy is armor for the soul
en.cta: Practice the 'View from Above.' Imagine looking at yourself from space. How small does your problem look?
en.summary: You've explored Stoicism (Control), Existentialism (Freedom), Nihilism, Virtue Ethics, and finding your Why.

18-35.title: Ethics in the Modern World: AI, Bioethics & Justice
18-35.description: Applying moral philosophy to contemporary challenges

en.title: Ethics in the Modern World: AI, Bioethics & Justice
en.welcome: Technology moves fast. Ethics moves slow. We are building gods (AI) and editing life (CRISPR) with the wisdom of apes. We need to upgrade our moral software.
en.mainContent:
**Utilitarianism (Mill):** The greatest good for the greatest number. 
*   *AI Car Problem:* Should a self-driving car swerve to save 5 pedestrians if it kills the 1 passenger? Utilitarian says yes. But would you buy that car?

**Deontology (Kant):** Rules and Duties. Some things are wrong, no matter the outcome. 
*   *Privacy:* Is it okay for the government to spy on everyone to catch one terrorist? Kant says no; privacy is a right. The ends do not justify the means.

**Bioethics (CRISPR):** We can now edit DNA. 
*   *Curing Disease:* Good! No more Cystic Fibrosis.
*   *Designer Babies:* Bad? Rich people buying taller, smarter kids. This creates a biological caste system.

**AI Ethics:** 
*   **Bias:** If AI learns from the internet, it learns our racism and sexism. 
*   **Alignment:** How do we ensure AI wants what we want? (The Paperclip Maximizer: An AI told to make paperclips might turn the whole universe into paperclips, including us).

**Social Justice (Rawls):** The Veil of Ignorance. Design a society without knowing who you will be in it (rich/poor, black/white, male/female). You would design a fair society because you might be the person at the bottom.

**Environmental Ethics:** Do we have a duty to future generations? To animals? Is nature a resource to use or a community to belong to?
keyPoints: Utilitarianism (Results) vs Deontology (Rules)
Bioethics: Just because we CAN do it, SHOULD we?
AI Ethics: Bias, Alignment, and the Paperclip Maximizer
Rawls' Veil of Ignorance: A tool for designing fairness
We need to expand our circle of moral concern (animals, future humans)
interactionPrompts: Would you buy a self-driving car that would sacrifice you to save others?
Should parents be allowed to choose their baby's eye color?
If you didn't know if you'd be rich or poor, what laws would you make?
en.wisdomMoment: Science tells us what we can do; Ethics tells us what we should do. Without ethics, science is a monster.
en.core_metaphor: Ethics is the steering wheel for technology
en.cta: Read about the 'Trolley Problem' variations. Discuss with a friend. See if you agree.
en.summary: You've explored Utilitarianism, Deontology, Bioethics (CRISPR), AI Ethics, Social Justice (Rawls), and Environmental Ethics.

36-60.title: Wisdom Traditions: Perennial Philosophy
36-60.description: Finding the common threads in the world's great spiritual and philosophical traditions

en.title: Wisdom Traditions: Perennial Philosophy
en.welcome: Aldous Huxley called it the 'Perennial Philosophy'—the idea that all great traditions (Buddhism, Christianity, Taoism, Stoicism) point to the same ultimate truth. Let's find the center.
en.mainContent:
**The Ego is the Problem:** Almost every tradition agrees: The 'Self' (Ego) is the source of suffering. 
*   *Buddhism:* Attachment to self causes Dukkha (suffering).
*   *Christianity:* Pride (self-love) is the root of sin.
*   *Solution:* Transcend the ego. Serve others. Humility.

**The Present Moment:** 
*   *Stoicism:* Focus on the now.
*   *Taoism:* Flow with the river (Wu Wei).
*   *Mindfulness:* Be here now.
Anxiety lives in the future. Regret lives in the past. Peace lives in the present.

**Interconnection:**
*   *Ubuntu (Africa):* 'I am because we are.'
*   *Indra's Net (Hinduism):* Everything reflects everything else.
*   *Ecology:* We are part of the web of life.
Separation is an illusion. We are one.

**Compassion:** The Golden Rule appears in every religion. 
*   *Islam:* None of you has faith until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
*   *Confucianism:* Do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself.
Compassion is the universal language.

**Surrender:** You are not in control. 
*   *Islam:* Means 'Surrender' (to God).
*   *Taoism:* Yield to overcome.
*   *AA (12 Steps):* Turn it over to a Higher Power.
Fighting reality causes pain. Acceptance brings peace.
keyPoints: Perennial Philosophy: Common truths across traditions
The Ego/Self is the source of suffering
Peace is found in the Present Moment
We are Interconnected (Ubuntu, Indra's Net)
Compassion and Surrender are universal paths to wisdom
interactionPrompts: Which tradition resonates most with you?
When have you felt 'connected' to everything?
What does 'Surrender' mean to you?
en.wisdomMoment: Truth is one; the sages call it by many names. (Rig Veda). Don't fight over the name; drink the water.
en.cta: Read one quote from a tradition you don't know (e.g., Rumi, Lao Tzu, St. Francis). Find the truth in it.
en.summary: You've explored Perennial Philosophy, Ego, Present Moment, Interconnection, Compassion, and Surrender.

61-102.title: The Examined Life: Meaning & Mortality
61-102.description: Reflecting on the journey, facing death, and finding peace

en.title: The Examined Life: Meaning & Mortality
en.welcome: Socrates said, 'The unexamined life is not worth living.' Now, looking back, we examine the tapestry. What does it mean? And what comes next?
en.mainContent:
**Meaning Making:** Meaning is not found; it is made. You make it by telling your story. The hardships were not punishments; they were plot twists. The losses were not failures; they were lessons. You are the author.

**Mortality (Memento Mori):** Remember you will die. This is not morbid; it is vital. Death gives life value. Scarcity creates value. If life were endless, it would be meaningless. The deadline makes the project real.

**Regrets of the Dying (Bronnie Ware):**
1.  I wish I'd had the courage to live a life true to myself, not what others expected.
2.  I wish I hadn't worked so hard.
3.  I wish I'd had the courage to express my feelings.
4.  I wish I had stayed in touch with my friends.
5.  I wish that I had let myself be happier.
Use this list as a checklist. It's not too late.

**Transcendence:** As the body fades, the spirit can soar. You are moving from 'Doing' to 'Being.' From 'Ambition' to 'Acceptance.' This is the final developmental stage (Erikson: Integrity vs. Despair).

**The Ripple Effect:** You will be forgotten. Your name will fade. But your ripples will not. Every act of kindness continues forever. You are part of the chain of being.

**Peace:** Peace comes when you stop fighting the river. Let go. Trust the process. You are safe.
keyPoints: Meaning is made by interpreting your life story
Memento Mori: Awareness of death makes life precious
Top 5 Regrets of the Dying (Live true, work less, love more)
Transcendence: Moving from Doing to Being
Your ripples continue even after your name is forgotten
interactionPrompts: Which of the 5 Regrets resonates most with you?
What is the 'theme' of your life story?
Are you ready to let go?
en.wisdomMoment: Death is not extinguishing the light; it is only putting out the lamp because the dawn has come. (Tagore).
en.core_metaphor: Life is a tapestry; death is the frame
en.cta: Write your own epitaph. Not what you did, but who you were. 'Here lies [Name], who loved...'
en.summary: You've explored Meaning Making, Memento Mori, Regrets of the Dying, Transcendence, The Ripple Effect, and Peace.
